meta.title: PingNow: Making it easier to get your golf group onto the course
meta.summary: TL;DR: I built PingNow, a group tee-time alert service for Bay Area golfers. Instead of just notifying individuals when a slot becomes available, PingNow helps an entire group find a time that works for everyone. Built with a technical teammate over four weeks, it grew into a live website and app covering around 40 public golf courses.

content.text: The problem wasn’t finding a tee time
I love playing golf. It’s my way of touching grass and keeping sane through otherwise busy weeks.

When I moved to San Francisco, I quickly discovered that getting a Saturday morning tee time at some of the Bay Area’s public courses was surprisingly difficult. At Presidio Golf Course, for example, the good slots could disappear within minutes of becoming available, and cancellations were often the only second chance.
But finding an available slot was only half the problem.

You still needed your group of golfers to agree on it. Someone would refresh a booking website, screenshot a handful of options, send them to the group chat, chase everyone for a response, and refresh again (
can you guess who that was in my group?
). By the time everyone agreed, the tee time was usually gone. Ugh.

It struck me that most existing solutions were addressing the wrong half of the problem. There were already services like RapidTee notifying individual golfers when tee times became available. But an alert is only useful if you can actually get your group onto the course.
The opportunity was to build around the group, not the individual.
Making the round the starting point
That became the central idea behind PingNow.

Instead of setting up individual alerts and coordinating over iMessage, you create a round with your friends, preferred courses, date and time window. PingNow monitors those courses and notifies everyone when a matching tee time becomes available.
The group then has a shared board of available options. Everyone marks the times that work for them, and once everyone agrees on a slot, someone can book directly through the course’s website.
Simple enough in theory! But there were interesting product decisions along the way.

The first version looked much like any other alert app: individual tee time watches, a separate alerts tab and a friends list. The group was there, but it wasn’t central to the experience: the alert told everyone that a tee time was available but it didn’t tell anyone whether the group could
actually
play. People still had to leave the app, discuss their availability in iMessage, and coordinate who would book. We had made it easier to find a tee time, but not much easier to organize a round.
So we rebuilt the product around a different concept:
the round

A round represents the group’s intention to play. It brings together what v1 kept apart (the watches, the alerts tab and the friends list), so the alert follows the round instead of living on its own. When a tee time opens up, it lands on the shared board described above, where everyone can mark whether it works.
The difference was that the coordination now happened inside the product. Instead of an alert being the end of the experience, it became the start of a shared decision.
